analysis.one_liner: Bars bankruptcy courts from cutting health benefits owed to retired union coal miners.
analysis.headline: The bill to protect retired miners' health coverage in bankruptcy never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a coal company goes bankrupt, bankruptcy courts can let it stop paying health benefits promised to retired miners and their families. This bill would change federal bankruptcy law so courts could not terminate or modify those benefits when the company is the last operator still obligated under a coal wage agreement. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, never received any further action, and died at the end of the 109th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Retired union coal miners, their spouses, and dependents who depend on company-paid health coverage. Federal law (chapter 99 of the Internal Revenue Code, the Coal Industry Retiree Health Benefit Act) obligates the last signatory coal operator to keep providing these benefits, but a bankruptcy court could currently modify or terminate them; this bill would take that option away, keeping retirees' coverage intact even if their former employer reorganizes under Chapter 11.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retired union coal miners and families

how_it_helps.text: Adds a subsection to bankruptcy law (11 U.S.C. § 1114) providing that benefits a last signatory coal operator must provide under chapter 99 of the Internal Revenue Code 'may not be terminated or modified by any court in a proceeding under this title' [S3].
The bill targets exactly the situation where a bankruptcy court could otherwise terminate or modify a Chapter 11 debtor-employer's coal industry retiree health benefits [S2].
Retired miners and their dependents whose coverage depends on these obligations would keep their health benefits even if their former employer files for bankruptcy reorganization.

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies that carry last-signatory obligations under a coal wage agreement: in a Chapter 11 bankruptcy they could no longer use the bankruptcy process to shed or reduce retiree health costs, so those obligations would remain on their books. Shareholders and creditors of such companies bear that cost indirectly.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a cost on coal companies in bankruptcy and their creditors, who under current law can treat retiree health obligations as debts that may be adjusted in reorganization; the bill makes those obligations untouchable, adding to the company's liabilities in a financial distress situation [S2, S3].

It is a narrow fix: it protects only benefits owed by the last signatory operator under the coal wage agreement framework, leaving other bankrupt companies' retiree benefits without similar protection [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and human: retired miners and their families keep health coverage they were promised and many cannot replace, even when their employer's finances collapse. The cost falls on a small set of coal operators and their creditors, and only in bankruptcy. The main weakness is design, not cost: the protection is limited to the last-signatory framework and does nothing for retirees of operators outside it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it; it died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter (R-PA) introduced S. 594 on March 10, 2005, with introductory remarks recorded in the Congressional Record [S1, S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that was the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal operators and their creditors benefit from the status quo: because the bill never became law, a coal company that files for bankruptcy can still ask a court to reduce or terminate its retiree health benefit obligations. Retired miners remain exposed to that risk.

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on March 10, 2005

for.name: One Senate Democrat and one Senate Republican

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 10, 2005 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator from coal country introduced the bill and it drew cosponsors from both parties (one Democrat, one Republican); no party blocked it on the record — it simply never moved.

industries.industry: Coal operators with last-signatory retiree obligations
industries.note: The bill would prevent these companies from using bankruptcy to terminate or modify retiree health benefits they are required to provide under the coal wage agreement framework, keeping those liabilities in place. For retired miners, that obligation is their health coverage.

industries.industry: Bankruptcy-reliant distressed coal companies and their creditors
industries.note: Under current bankruptcy law, retiree health obligations can be adjusted in a Chapter 11 reorganization; this bill would exempt coal retiree benefits from that adjustment, raising the cost of reorganizing.
